sentences.text: Australosuchus clarkae is the type species of an extinct genus of crocodylian known as Australosuchus.
The name combines Latin and Greek roots to mean "southern crocodile," reflecting its unique geographic position.
Willis estimated the length of this animal to be around 3 meters, featuring a moderately broad and flattened skull.
The upper jaw contained 14 teeth on each side, while the lower jaw held between 16 and 17 teeth.
A distinct feature was the vestigial fifth toe, which was robust and thicker than in other crocodilians.
Australosuchus held the southernmost distribution of any mekosuchine, found only below 27°S latitude.
Its southern range far exceeds the latitude of any modern crocodilian, such as the American alligator which ranges up to 36°N.
Fossils of Australosuchus were mentioned in literature as early as 1968, before the genus was formally described.
The genus was named by Willis and Molnar in 1991.
Fossils were discovered at Lake Palankarinna within the Etadunna Formation near the same lake.
The holotype specimen QM F16788 is a partial skeleton collected in 1975.
The species name clarkae honors Elaine Clark.
Researchers suggest Australosuchus was cold-resistant, allowing it to live in freshwater systems too cold for other crocodilians.
Due to the lack of specialized adaptations like ziphodont teeth or a longirostrine skull, it is thought to have been a generalized member of Mekosuchinae.
It belongs to the subfamily Mekosuchinae.
Australosuchus lived during the Late Oligocene and Early Miocene epochs.
It lived between 27.3 and 15.98 million years ago.
Australosuchus clarkae inhabited the Lake Eyre Basin in South Australia.
It is debated whether some fossils belong to the Mampuwordu Sands (Late Pliocene to Early Pleistocene) or were reworked from older strata.
A 2021 morphological analysis by Rio and Mannion placed Australosuchus outside Mekosuchinae as the sister taxon to Crocodylidae.
Some phylogenetic analyses suggest Kalthifrons or a clade of Kalthifrons and Kambara might be more basal than Australosuchus.
